title: Fantastic Generalization Measures and Where to Find Them
publication_status_observed: ICLR 2020 (arXiv preprint dated Dec 2019, presented at ICLR 2020)
main_claims: Sharpness-based measures (PAC-Bayesian bounds and the Keskar et al. sharpness measure) exhibit the highest correlation with generalization gap among 40+ complexity measures studied.
Many norm-based measures negatively correlate with generalization when optimizers inject stochasticity, rendering them unreliable.
Spurious correlations in generalization studies can be mitigated by using granulated Kendall's coefficient, which controls for hyperparameter axes.
methodology: Over 10,000 convolutional networks were trained on CIFAR-10 and SVHN by systematically varying 7 hyperparameters (batch size, dropout, learning rate, depth, weight decay, width, optimizer). More than 40 complexity measures from theoretical and empirical literature were evaluated using Kendall rank correlation and a novel granulated Kendall coefficient that controls for individual hyperparameter axes.
key_results: Sharpness-based measures (PAC-Bayes and Keskar sharpness) have highest overall correlation (granulated Kendall's Ψ) with generalization gap across all studied measures.
Spectral-norm-based bounds show strong negative correlation with generalization in the presence of stochastic optimizers.
Optimization-based measures (gradient noise, optimization speed) are also predictive of generalization.
limitations: Correlation analysis cannot establish causal relationships between complexity measures and generalization.
Models are limited to convolutional architectures on CIFAR-10 and SVHN; conclusions may not extend to other architectures or tasks.
Measures are computed on sufficiently but not necessarily fully trained models.
relevance_to_rq: This paper directly supports the RQ's premise: sharpness-based measures are the strongest empirical correlates of generalization gap, justifying SAM's sharpness-reduction objective. However, the correlational nature of the evidence (the paper's own limitation) is exactly what the RQ probes—CKA stability may track OOD generalization more tightly than sharpness alone.

key_quotes.text: Sharpness-based measures such as PAC-Bayesian bounds and sharpness measure proposed by Keskar et al. (2016) perform the best overall and seem to be promising candidates for further research.
key_quotes.context: Summary of main finding on sharpness as a generalization predictor

key_quotes.text: Many norm-based measures not only perform poorly, but negatively correlate with generalization specifically when the optimization procedure injects some stochasticity.
key_quotes.context: Finding on norm-based measures failing under stochastic optimizers

key_quotes.text: empirical correlation does not necessarily translate to a casual relationship between a measure and generalization.
key_quotes.context: Key limitation of correlation-based analysis of complexity measures
